cite: Proulx, G. (1995). Evacuation time and movement in apartment buildings. Fire Safety Journal 24(3), 229-246.
finding: Four apartment drills. Alarm audibility dominated time to start (169 s audible vs 515 s poor). 62% evacuated in groups, mostly pairs or threes, at the slowest member's pace. Residents chose familiar stairs over the nearest.
notes: Announced drills in 6-7 storey buildings, so a real fire is likely slower. Citation carried from the project's evidence ledger; not yet read first-hand for this registry.

cite: Proulx, G. and Fahy, R. (1997). The time delay to start evacuation: review of five case studies. Fire Safety Science 5, 783-794.
finding: Residential time to start 169 s with a good alarm, 515 s with a poor one; pre-movement was about two thirds of total evacuation time. At Forest Laneway 24% did not hear the alarm.
notes: Citation carried from the project's evidence ledger; not yet read first-hand for this registry.

cite: Lovreglio, R., Kuligowski, E., Gwynne, S. and Boyce, K. (2019). A pre-evacuation database for use in egress simulations. Fire Safety Journal 105, 107-128.
finding: Fitted residential pre-evacuation distributions: good-alarm cluster Weibull scale 102.475 s shape 0.767 (n=149); poor-alarm or real-fire cluster Weibull scale 724.617 s shape 0.978 (n=78).
notes: The lognormal rows of the same table are internally inconsistent between units; use the Weibull or gamma rows. Citation carried from the project's evidence ledger.

cite: Averill, J. et al. (2005). Occupant behavior, egress, and emergency communications. NIST NCSTAR 1-7, World Trade Center Investigation.
finding: About 70% of occupants milled - sought information or conferred - before evacuating. 30-34% helped others; 23-32% searched for others. Cues such as smoke made people leave slower, not faster, because they triggered sense-making first.
notes: An office population, so group and family effects transfer poorly to a residential tower. URL not yet recorded.

cite: Kuligowski, E. (2009). The process of human behavior in fires. NIST Technical Note 1632.
finding: Sets out the perception-interpretation-decision-action model the TTS side of this project is built on.

cite: SFPE Handbook of Fire Protection Engineering, movement chapters, following Fruin's pedestrian planning work.
finding: Able-bodied adults walk about 1.19-1.25 m/s on the level; older adults are markedly slower; children are slower; assisted occupants much slower.
notes: Named in a comment on the team's first workbook. Edition, chapter and page still to be pinned down.

cite: Bohannon, R. (2008). Comfortable and maximum walking speed of adults aged 20-79 years: reference values and determinants.
finding: Comfortable adult walking speed about 1.20 m/s with a standard deviation near 0.24 m/s.
notes: Citation carried from the project's evidence ledger; the standard deviation matters here because it is the spread this registry samples.

cite: Controlled stair-descent trials with older adults, Fire Technology (2024).
finding: Stair descent speeds for older adults are well below the able-bodied adult figures usually quoted.
notes: Named in a comment on the team's first workbook. Authors, title and volume still to be pinned down.

cite: Jin, T. (1978). Visibility through fire smoke.
finding: Walking speed falls as smoke reduces visibility; in irritant smoke people slow to about 0.3 m/s.
notes: Named in a comment on the team's first workbook.

cite: Fridolf, K., Nilsson, D. and Frantzich, H. (2013). Movement speed and exit choice in smoke-filled rail tunnels.
finding: In dense smoke people slow to around 0.3 m/s and may crawl or follow a wall.
notes: Named in a comment on the team's first workbook.

cite: Frantzich, H. and Nilsson, D. (2003). Utvardering av forsok med utrymning i rokfylld tunnel (Evacuation experiments in a smoke-filled tunnel).
finding: Speed-visibility relationships in smoke used for the smoke speed-reduction factors.
notes: Named in a comment on the team's first workbook.

cite: US Census Bureau, American Community Survey, table B11016 (household type by household size), San Francisco.
finding: San Francisco households of 1 / 2 / 3 / 4-or-more people are 40.65 / 32.67 / 12.12 / 14.57 percent.
notes: Five-and-more folded into four. Flats in large buildings hold fewer people than the city average, which is why the occupancy target here is stated per flat and the size weights are tilted to match it.

cite: US Census Bureau, American Community Survey, table B18105 (ambulatory difficulty by age).
finding: Ambulatory difficulty runs about 3.8 percent among adults aged 35-64 and about 18.2 percent among those 65 and over.
notes: This is the share the workbook's 'mobility impaired' category actually matches - not the much smaller wheelchair share.

cite: US Census Bureau, Survey of Income and Program Participation, wheelchair and mobility device use.
finding: About 1.3 percent of the adult population uses a wheelchair.

cite: Fire on Floor 12 - what do I do? First-person walkthrough by the project team, three positions relative to the fire floor.
finding: Below the fire: alarm-only cue, assume a false alarm, check the hallway, the phone and the building group chat before leaving. On the fire floor: multi-sensory cues, alert the household, call 999/911 while moving, take the far stair. Above: cues delayed, contact people in the building, consider knocking on neighbours, shelter and seal if the stair is not clear.
notes: Recorded in context.md section 5. This is the only source for the building group chat as a warning channel, which is why those rows are INVENTED rather than ESTIMATE.
